opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most underappreciated problems in the whole space. When people think about AI for engineering, they tend to picture code generation, an agent writing a function or fixing a bug. But if you sit with engineers at a large company and watch how they spend their day, most of the time isn't spent writing code. It's spent trying to understand things. Why was this system designed this way? Who owns this service? What happened the last time someone touched this config? That knowledge is scattered across the codebase, design docs, Slack threads, tickets, postmortems, and a lot of it lives only in people's heads.

So my view is that the right AI tool for an organization like that has to start with comprehension, not generation. It needs to ingest all of those sources, not just the repo, and build a real understanding of how they connect. A code snippet on its own is often meaningless without the conversation that explains why it exists.

The second piece, which I think is really important, is that the system should learn from the team over time. In any big org there's tribal knowledge that was never written down. The senior engineer knows you don't touch a certain module on Fridays, or that a particular test is flaky and can be ignored. A good system should let people teach it those things and keep them, so the knowledge becomes institutional instead of disappearing when someone changes teams or leaves.

And then there's an agentic research piece. Answering a hard question about a big system isn't one retrieval step. It's more like what a strong engineer does: look at the code, follow a reference, check the ticket history, form a hypothesis, then verify it. We've found that when you give models the ability to do that kind of multi-step investigation, with long context and good tools, the quality of the answers changes dramatically compared to simple RAG.

Ultimately I think that's the foundation for the more autonomous future everyone's excited about. You can't trust an agent to make meaningful changes to a complex system it doesn't understand. Getting the understanding right is the prerequisite for everything else.

r001.rationale: The response describes large companies and complex systems, but never says the codebase is beyond any individual engineer’s ability to understand in full.

r002.rationale: It explicitly locates engineering knowledge in design docs, Slack threads, tickets, postmortems, and people’s heads, beyond the codebase.

r003.rationale: It advocates multi-step research modeled on a strong engineer, but does not say the tool should answer with the understanding of the organization’s most deeply embedded expert.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually the core problem. If you look at how people have thought about AI for engineering, the mental model has mostly been "autocomplete, but better" — you're sitting in your editor, and the model predicts the next few lines. And that's useful, but it's solving a pretty narrow problem. In a real engineering org, the hard part was never typing the code. The hard part is that the knowledge you need to make a good decision is spread across a hundred places. It's in the codebase, sure, but it's also in Slack threads from two years ago, in a design doc that nobody updated, in a Jira ticket, in the head of the one person who built the service and then moved teams.

So when a new engineer joins, what actually happens is they spend months just building a mental map of where things are and why they are the way they are. And even senior people, when they go into an unfamiliar part of the system, they're kind of acting like a new hire again. They go ask around, they read old PRs, they piece it together.

What I think AI should do is basically act as that map. Not just read the code, but understand the organization — the history, the conversations, the decisions that were made and the reasons behind them. The way I'd frame it is the model needs to have the context of a senior engineer who's been at the company for five years, and it needs to have that context on day one and keep it current as things change.

And there are a few things that fall out of that. One is you have to actually connect to all those sources — the code, the docs, the chat, the tickets — and build a kind of living representation of the organization rather than treating each as a separate search problem. Two, the model has to be able to reason over that, not just retrieve from it. If somebody asks "why does this service retry three times instead of five," the answer isn't in any single document; it's a Slack conversation plus a postmortem plus a commit message, and you have to synthesize. And three, it has to be something the whole team shares. If it's just a personal assistant for one developer, the knowledge stays fragmented. The value really comes when it becomes a shared layer that everyone's interacting with and contributing to.

The longer-term version of this is that engineers stop spending their time on archaeology and spend it on the actual engineering judgment. That's where I think the big productivity unlock is — not in writing code faster, but in collapsing the time it takes to understand enough to make a good decision.

r001.rationale: The response describes knowledge spread across many sources and difficulty understanding unfamiliar systems, but does not identify organizations whose codebase complexity and team size exceed any one engineer’s ability to understand the full codebase.

r002.rationale: It explicitly places engineering knowledge in Slack threads, design docs, Jira tickets, and conversations, as well as in the codebase.

r003.rationale: It says the model should have the context of a senior engineer who has been at the company for five years, available on day one and kept current.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that an engineering organization knows a lot more than any individual in it, but that knowledge is fragmented. Some of it is in code, some is in documents, and some is in the head of the person who remembers why a decision was made two years ago.

An AI tool should help bring the relevant pieces together around the problem you’re solving. If you’re changing a system, you don’t just want to find its documentation. You want to understand what depends on it, what constraints shaped it, and who might know something that isn’t written down.

The difficult part is knowing which information to trust. A document might be outdated; the code might reflect a workaround rather than the intended design. So the tool needs to show where its understanding comes from, recognize conflicting evidence, and ask for clarification when it matters. That’s how you make organizational knowledge useful without turning scattered, uncertain information into a very confident wrong answer.

r001.rationale: The response says the organization knows more than any individual and that knowledge is fragmented, but it does not identify codebase complexity and team size as the reasons no engineer can understand the entire codebase.

r002.rationale: It mentions documents and people’s memories, but does not specify organizational communication or project management tools as places where engineering knowledge resides outside the codebase.

r003.rationale: It proposes bringing relevant information together and identifying who may know undocumented details, but does not say the AI should answer with the understanding of the organization’s most deeply embedded human expert.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that an engineering organization knows a lot more than any one person in it. Some of that knowledge is in code, some is in design docs, and some is in a conversation where somebody explained why a decision was made. The hard part is connecting those pieces to the problem you’re working on right now.

So an AI tool should be able to follow those connections. If I ask why a system behaves a certain way, it should find the relevant code, trace the decision behind it, and show me what supports its answer. And it needs to respect permissions and recognize when a document is stale or two sources disagree.

That’s where I think these tools can become really useful: helping you recover the context you would otherwise have to get by finding the right person and asking them a series of questions.

r001.rationale: The response says an organization knows more than any one person, but does not identify the target scope as organizations whose codebase complexity and team size make the entire codebase impossible for an individual engineer to understand.

r002.rationale: It explicitly places some knowledge in conversations explaining why decisions were made, locating organizational knowledge outside the codebase in communication.

r003.rationale: The response says AI can help recover context that might otherwise require asking the right person, but does not propose that it answer with the understanding of the organization’s most deeply embedded human expert.
